title: The thaw feeds the sponges
hook: Melting ice washes ground-up rock into the sea. Its phosphorus feeds a bloom of algae and sponges, and the mass of living things grows more than fourfold.

title: Life fills the open sea
hook: Animals rise off the seafloor into open water, where giant shelled relatives of squid hunt. Sea animal families triple, and nerve signaling grows about sixfold.

title: The sea refills
hook: The ice melts and the seas lose oxygen for a while. Then sea scorpions and early jawed fish spread into the emptied water, and nerve signaling triples.

title: Reefs and armored fish collapse
hook: The first forests wash nutrients into the sea, which then runs short of oxygen. About 75% of sea species die, including the armored fish, and nerve signaling falls by 70%.

title: Egg-layers take the land
hook: The shelled egg lets reptile and mammal ancestors breed far from water. Herds of tusked plant-eaters roam seed-fern forests, just before the worst extinction ever.

title: Life in thin air
hook: Oxygen is down to about 14%, and good breathers win. Dinosaur ancestors get one-way airflow lungs; mammal ancestors get nose bones that save heat and water, a step toward warm blood.

title: Dinosaurs rise on two legs
hook: A long rainy spell reshapes the land. The first dinosaurs run on two legs, which takes a sharper sense of balance, and nerve signaling grows fourfold.

title: Warm blood and a layered cortex
Volcanoes clear the field
hook: Huge eruptions, as the Atlantic starts to open, fill the air with carbon dioxide. About 76% of species die, and dinosaurs rule the land for the next 135 million years.

title: First flowers and pollinators
hook: Flowering plants advertise with petals, scent and nectar so insects fly pollen straight to the next bloom, multiplying plant diversity.

title: A hothouse of new mammals
hook: The warmest stretch since the dinosaurs died. Early primates and the ancestors of whales and carnivores spread out, some brains start to fold, and nerve signaling more than doubles.

title: Sperm-whale clans and savannas
hook: Deep-diving sperm whales evolve 8-kilogram brains and learned click dialects while songbirds sing for mates and open grasslands spread.

title: Apes stand up
hook: East Africa dries out and grasslands spread. Our line splits from the chimpanzees', and our ancestors start walking upright, which frees their hands.

title: A toolmaking tradition
hook: Homo habilis strikes sharp flakes to cut meat and crack bones for marrow. Each flake outlasts its maker by a million years, and memory stored outside bodies grows tenfold.

title: Bigger brains, planned tools
hook: Neanderthals and their relatives hunt big game with wooden spears and shape stone in several planned steps. Their brains reach 1,200–1,450 cm³, as big as ours.

title: The first Homo sapiens
hook: Across Africa, early Homo sapiens at sites like Jebel Irhoud combine modern-sized skulls, prepared-core stone blades and three-generation family bands.

title: The first symbols
hook: In Blombos Cave, South Africa, people scratch a crosshatch into red ochre and wear shell beads. Marks now carry meaning, and memory outside bodies grows tenfold.

title: Farming and villages
hook: People in the Fertile Crescent plant wheat, tame goats and cattle, and settle down. About half the kinds of large mammals disappear while farms and herds spread.

title: Clay tokens become signs
hook: Traders seal counting tokens inside clay balls, then press the tokens into the outside to show what is in. Objects become flat marks, one step before writing.

title: The alphabet
hook: Writers around Sinai and Phoenicia shrink about 800 word-signs to 22 letters, one per sound, so reading gets far easier to learn. In China, Shang kings carve questions into oracle bones.

title: Rules for reasoning
hook: In India, Panini writes about 4,000 exact rules for Sanskrit grammar. Greeks prove geometry step by step, and coins put a number on value. Reasoning gets written rules.

title: Libraries and empires
hook: The Library of Alexandria collects tens of thousands of scrolls or more (ancient writers give 40,000 to 700,000), and Callimachus makes a catalog to find them. Euclid writes the Elements, and bronze gears predict eclipses.

title: The book with pages
hook: Bound pages replace scrolls. With page numbers and a table of contents, you can jump straight to any passage instead of unrolling to it.

title: Paper and zero
hook: Paper mills spread from Samarkand to Baghdad and Córdoba. Numbers with a zero turn hard sums into quick written steps, and in China Bi Sheng prints with clay type.

title: Science goes public
hook: The first science journal appears in 1665. Printed log tables turn multiplying into adding, and Pascal and Leibniz build calculators with gears. Results become public and checkable.

title: Machines count the census
hook: Punch-card machines count the 1890 US census. Cheap wood-pulp paper floods the world but crumbles within decades, and radio starts sending messages without wires.

title: Microchips and networks
hook: Whole circuits now fit on one silicon chip, and Gordon Moore predicts the count will keep doubling. Data moves to magnetic tape and disk, and ARPANET links computers by sending data in packets.

title: Smartphones and synthetic cells
hook: Pocket smartphones connect a billion people to cameras, maps and cloud servers while chemists synthesize a million-letter genome that boots a living cell.

title: Language machines
hook: Transformer models trained on huge amounts of text learn to write. AlphaFold predicts the shapes of about 200 million proteins: silicon starts reading biology.
